bass-popper:
How to tie a Bass Popper. Few things in fishing beat a bass blowing up on a popper. This simple version uses a ready-made foam head, a feathered tail and rubber legs, so you can tie a box full in an evening.

You'll need a popper hook, size two to six. Strong three-oh thread. Marabou and a hackle feather for the tail, a foam popper head, and silicone skirt legs.

Step one. Start the thread at the bend, and tie in a marabou tail with a hackle feather on each side.

Step two. Wrap a thread base on the shank, add glue, and push the foam popper head onto the hook so it sits right behind the eye.

Step three. Push a few silicone legs through the foam or tie them in behind the head, then trim them to length.

Pop it, then pause, along weed lines and lily pads. Most strikes come while it's sitting still.

dahlberg-diver:
How to tie a Dahlberg Diver. Larry Dahlberg's deer hair bug floats at rest, dives and wiggles when you strip it, then pops back up. Bass and pike can't stand it. It takes some practice spinning hair, but it's worth it.

You'll need a bass bug hook, size one-aught to six. Strong three-oh thread. Marabou and flash for the tail, deer hair for the body and collar, and stiff mono for an optional weedguard.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a full marabou tail with a few strands of flash.

Step two. Spin bunches of deer hair over the front half of the shank, packing each one back tightly.

Step three. Clip the hair to shape: flat underneath, a flat face at the front, and a flared collar that slopes back. The collar is what makes it dive.

Step four. Whip finish, and add a mono weedguard if you'll fish it in heavy cover.

Strip, pause, and strip again around weed beds and lily pads. Let it pop back up between strips.

foam-spider:
How to tie a Foam Spider. This little bream bug is just a strip of foam and some rubber legs, and it might be the best way to introduce a kid to fly fishing. Bluegill and other sunfish smash it all summer.

You'll need a size ten dry fly or popper hook. Six-oh thread to match. A strip of two-millimeter closed-cell foam, fine round rubber legs, optional dubbing for an underbody, and super glue.

Step one. Lay a thread base along the shank and add a drop of super glue.

Step two. Cut a strip of foam about as wide as the hook gap, and tie it on top of the shank at the middle.

Step three. At the same spot, tie in two rubber legs on each side with figure-eight wraps.

Step four. If you want a little color under the foam, dub a small underbody.

Step five. Whip finish at the waist, then trim the foam ends into a rounded head and tail.

Step six. Trim the legs to about one and a half body lengths.

Cast close to grass edges and cypress knees. Let it sit until the rings disappear, then give it a twitch. Chartreuse, black and yellow all work.

murdich-minnow:
How to tie a Murdich Minnow. Bill Murdich's baitfish has a flashy braid body, a slim synthetic wing and a resin-coated head. It's tough, it casts well, and stripers, bluefish and albies hammer it.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size one to two-aught. White three-oh thread. Pearl flash braid for the body, synthetic fiber for the wing, stick-on eyes, and epoxy or UV resin.

Step one. Start the thread and wrap a pearl flash braid body over most of the shank.

Step two. Tie in the synthetic wing in thin layers, light colors on the bottom and darker on top, tapering toward the tail.

Step three. Add a stick-on eye on each side of the head, then coat the head with epoxy or UV resin and cure it.

Strip it fast through schools of bait.

clouser-crayfish:
How to tie a Clouser Crayfish. Bob Clouser built this crayfish for smallmouth on the Susquehanna River. It has feather pincers, a segmented shell and a buggy body, and it's deadly on rocky bottoms.

You'll need a streamer hook, size four to eight. Olive six-oh thread. Lead-free wire for weight. Hen mallard or hen saddle feathers for the pincers, fine bucktail for the antennae, tan-olive dubbing with a grizzly hackle for the body, and mottled turkey for the shell.

Step one. Wrap lead-free wire along the shank, then flatten it with pliers so the crayfish is wide and flat.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a few strands of fine bucktail as antennae, then a feather on each side as the claws.

Step three. Tie in the turkey shell and a hackle, dub the body forward, and palmer the hackle through it. Pull the shell over the top and segment it with thread wraps.

Step four. Whip finish, and coat the shell with flexible cement.

Hop it along rocky bottoms for smallmouth bass.

hollow-fleye:
How to tie a Hollow Fleye. Bob Popovics's hollow-tie method makes a big, bulky baitfish from a little bucktail. The hair flares back around the shank, so the fly looks fat in the water but casts light.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size one-aught to four-aught. White three-oh thread. Bucktail in three or four bunches, flash, 3D eyes, and UV resin for the head.

Step one. At the bend, hollow-tie a bunch of bucktail: tips pointing forward around the shank, then fold them back with thread so they flare.

Step two. Move forward a little and hollow-tie the next bunch the same way, adding a few strands of flash between bunches.

Step three. Finish with a darker bunch on top for the back.

Step four. Glue on the eyes and add a drop of resin at the head.

Strip it for stripers, bluefish and false albacore wherever you find bait.

merkin-crab:
How to tie a Merkin Crab. Del Brown's yarn crab caught permit when nothing else would, and it's just as good for redfish and black drum. The yarn body sinks flat and lands softly.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size two to one-aught. Tan flat-waxed nylon thread. Lead or brass dumbbell eyes. Grizzly or tan hackle tips and a little flash for the claws. Tan and olive sparkle yarn, barred rubber legs, and flexible cement.

Step one. Lash the dumbbell eyes underneath the shank behind the hook eye, so the hook rides point-up.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a few strands of flash and two pairs of hackle tips splayed outward as claws.

Step three. Tie short pieces of yarn across the shank with figure-eight wraps, alternating colors, and work forward toward the eye. Pack them tightly.

Step four. Partway along, tie in two or three rubber legs on each side.

Step five. Finish the thread behind the eyes and whip finish.

Step six. Trim the yarn into a flat oval about the size of a quarter, and glue the underside lightly to hold it together.

Sight-cast to tailing redfish and black drum. Lead the fish, let the crab sink, and give it tiny strips.

bendback:
How to tie a Bendback. With a slight bend in the hook shank, this baitfish rides point-up and the wing covers the point, so you can drag it through grass and mangrove roots without getting snagged.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size two to two-aught. White or chartreuse three-oh thread. Pearl or silver braid for the body, bucktail or synthetic fiber with flash for the wing, and stick-on eyes if you like.

Step one. With pliers, bend the shank up slightly, about a third back from the eye.

Step two. Wrap a braid body from the hook bend up to the bend in the shank.

Step three. Turn the hook over, and tie in a sparse wing so it covers the hook point.

Step four. Add a little flash, stick-on eyes if you want them, and build a head. Coat it with UV resin.

Drag it through grass and mangrove roots for snook, redfish and seatrout, without hanging up.

surf-candy:
How to tie a Surf Candy. Bob Popovics's resin-coated baitfish is slim, translucent and nearly indestructible. It's a top fly when false albacore and bluefish are blitzing on small bait.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size one to two-aught. Clear mono thread. Pearl tinsel for the body, Ultra Hair or bucktail for the wing, stick-on eyes, and epoxy or UV resin.

Step one. Start the clear thread and wrap a pearl tinsel body.

Step two. Tie the wing in thin layers: lighter colors underneath, darker on top.

Step three. Add a stick-on eye on each side, then coat the front half of the fly with resin.

Step four. Shape the resin into a smooth baitfish head with your fingers or a tool, and cure it.

Strip it fast through bait schools for false albacore, bluefish, stripers and Spanish mackerel.

redfish-toad:
How to tie a Redfish Toad. This smaller cousin of the Tarpon Toad has a chenille head and a rabbit or marabou tail. It lands softly, sinks slowly and swims with a wiggle that redfish can't ignore.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size one to two. Thread to match. Lead dumbbell eyes, a rabbit strip or marabou for the tail, and chenille for the head.

Step one. Tie the dumbbell eyes on behind the hook eye, then tie in a rabbit strip or marabou tail at the bend.

Step two. Wrap chenille forward from the tail to the eyes and around them, then trim the head flat on top and bottom.

Fish it slowly near tailing redfish, with short strips and long pauses.
